title: Organisational invention: Cross-domain ties reshape institutions
desc: Uses banking and biotechnology to explain how boundary-crossing practices become network-supported forms, with tipping conditions unresolved.

kps.k: Organizational invention arises when practices crossing social domains reshape the networks that sustain them.
kps.d: The cluster offers a relational explanation of institutional change rather than treating organizations as fixed actors responding to technology. The Problem of Emergence and Padgett’s Florentine study distinguish local improvements from systemic invention by the extent of their spillovers. Transposition moves practices between domains; refunctionality gives them new purposes; catalysis occurs when feedback changes how surrounding relations reproduce. People’s careers, skills and continuing affiliations carry these effects. The distinction between innovation and invention remains a matter of degree, not a sharp boundary.

qs.q: Hence not autocatalysis within one network but interaction among autocatalytic networks is the key to generating novelty.
Recombinant in- novation in organizations is produced, this case study shows, when one or more social relations are transposed from one domain to another, mixing in use with relations already there.
qs.a: Transposition and Refunctionality: The Birth of Partnership Systems in Renaissance Florence · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Florentine partnerships illustrate a distinction between political origins and later social institutionalization.
kps.d: Padgett dates the partnership system’s emergence to 1383. He argues that post-Ciompi political incorporation brought domestic guild practices into international merchant finance, producing simultaneous, cross-industry partnerships with family and nonfamily managers. Logit regressions of partnership dyads associate political mobilization with formation during 1383–99; they do not establish that officeholding sustained the system afterward. Marriage and natal class later anchored its reproduction. Padgett interprets these ties as foundations for merchant trust and wider financial and political transformation, while marking his 1427 interpretation as provisional because relevant archival records remained uncoded. The Problem of Emergence draws on this same case rather than supplying independent confirmation.

qs.q: Specifically, the Florentine invention of the partnership system was a hybridization of the two relational logics of patrilineage and guild through the means of political republicanism.
qs.a: Transposition and Refunctionality: The Birth of Partnership Systems in Renaissance Florence · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Tables 6.6 and 6.7 present logit regressions on partnership dyads in these two industries over time.
qs.a: Transposition and Refunctionality: The Birth of Partnership Systems in Renaissance Florence · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Biotechnology extends the argument from new firms to geographically concentrated institutional communities.
kps.d: The Problem of Emergence reports Powell and Sandholtz’s account of scientist-entrepreneurs and venture capital moving laboratory practices into commerce in the 1970s, with reciprocal effects on science as patenting joined publishing as an output measure. It also reports Powell and Owen-Smith’s argument that multiple independent connections among diverse organizations sustained exploration. Organizational and Institutional Genesis argues that technological breakthroughs alone cannot explain why biotech clusters formed in particular places; changing affiliations and the normalization of new science–finance relationships also require explanation. Its supplied excerpt presents a theoretical proposition and research questions, not empirical results establishing that explanation.

qs.q: In chapter 13, Powell and Sandholtz document the transposition, via venture capital, of the scientific life-sciences lab from the univer- sity to the market, thereby making the dedicated biotechnology firm.

This Schumpeterian portrait of a process of creative destruction captures in broad brushstrokes the changed technological landscape, but it does not illumi- nate where the winds of change would be the strongest.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

kps.k: The central disagreement concerns technological sufficiency and inevitable progress, not whether technology matters.
kps.d: The sources broadly align rather than dispute one another. They challenge accounts that explain new institutions through breakthroughs, diffusion or replacement of incumbents alone. The Problem of Emergence recasts creative destruction as the breakup and replacement of networks and argues that invention can change the criteria by which organizations succeed. Padgett likewise rejects inevitable modernization: elites seeking to preserve threatened status can unintentionally generate transformative arrangements. These accounts therefore separate conservative intentions from potentially disruptive consequences.

qs.q: When selection environ- ments are endogenously molded by the innova- tions they select, however, performance criteria migrate, and “optimum” loses the supporting scale upon which it is defined.
Florentine elites invented not because they wanted to but because they had to, conser- vatively to preserve their threatened positions.
qs.a: Transposition and Refunctionality: The Birth of Partnership Systems in Renaissance Florence · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Network reinforcement can sustain both institutional resilience and resistance to novelty; tipping conditions remain unresolved.
kps.d: The Problem of Emergence uses autocatalytic models to explain how interacting networks reproduce and repair themselves. It distinguishes these model findings from historical evidence and treats biochemistry as an inspiration, not a literal social model. The authors propose that reduced network redundancy may permit cascading change, but excessive weakening may instead cause collapse. Crises therefore do not predict the institutions that follow. Padgett similarly acknowledges that his Florentine account explains mechanisms more fully than the initial structural conditions that made transformation possible.

qs.q: To explain the emergence of new organiza- tional actors, we take as our starting inspira- tion—but not as our final model—biochemical insights about the emergence of life.
This chapter has focused more on mechanism than on structural preconditions.
qs.a: Transposition and Refunctionality: The Birth of Partnership Systems in Renaissance Florence · Academia · 2012

kps.k: The practical implication is to study changing relationships over time, not infer institutional transformation from adoption alone.
kps.d: The sources direct researchers toward longitudinal evidence on careers, training, finance, political incorporation and other intersecting affiliations. Analysis should distinguish the relationships that generate a new form from those that later sustain it, and track whether practices merely spread or alter roles, purposes and surrounding institutions. This is a research strategy rather than a validated recipe for engineering clusters or forecasting organizational change. The supplied material does not directly test its applicability to contemporary legal services or AI.

qs.q: Study- ing organizational novelty places a premium on measuring multiple social networks in inter action because that is the raw material for re- lational recombination.

The empiri- cal chapters were selected on the basis of two criteria: (a) detailed multiple-network informa- tion, tracing not just actors but relations among actors; and (b) dynamic networks over time, spanning an observed organizational or market invention of interest.

vlens.an: These curated academia and research sources accept the principal proposition and materially develop it into a mechanism-based research programme. Their common reasoning is that organizational invention cannot be explained adequately by technological breakthroughs, adoption or diffusion alone: practices and relational protocols move across domains, acquire new functions, and become systemic when feedback alters the networks that reproduce them. They also distinguish the relationships responsible for genesis from those that later sustain and institutionalize a form, and agree that the structural conditions making a system susceptible to tipping remain less well established. There is material variation in contribution and evidential status. Padgett provides the most specific historical and quantitative evidence, separating the political genesis of Florentine partnerships from their later reproduction through marriage and social class, while marking parts of the later-period interpretation as provisional. The Problem of Emergence generalizes the relational account across historical cases and autocatalytic models, but presents model findings as suggestive rather than universal empirical laws. The biotech-cluster source extends the unit of explanation from organizations to geographically concentrated institutional communities and argues that changing network affiliations help explain location; however, the supplied excerpt states theory and research questions rather than completed empirical validation. Thus the sources collectively build on the proposition through mechanisms, case differentiation, extension of analytical scale and a longitudinal research strategy, without establishing a predictive theory of institutional change.

qs.q: Hence not autocatalysis within one network but interaction among autocatalytic networks is the key to generating novelty.
Here we take the next step and argue that changing logics of network af- filiation explain both the emergence of organiza- tions and the formation of regional communities.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundations strongly support the proposition that organisational invention occurs through cross-domain practices and the restructuring of the networks that sustain them. Across the curated sources, the common explanation is relational rather than technologically deterministic: people, practices and affiliations move between domains, acquire new functions and generate wider institutional effects through feedback. Padgett’s Florentine study supplies the principal historical mechanism and distinguishes the political genesis of partnership systems from their later reproduction through marriage and social class. The Problem of Emergence generalises this into a theory of interactions among self-reproducing networks and explains why established network reinforcement can both sustain institutions and resist novelty. The biotech-cluster source materially extends the same reasoning from individual organisational forms to regional communities, arguing that technological breakthroughs alone cannot explain geographic concentration. Material variation concerns scope and evidential status, not the core proposition: the Florentine account includes historical and regression evidence but flags provisional archival interpretation; The Problem of Emergence combines cases with models and leaves susceptibility to tipping unresolved; and the biotech excerpt advances a theoretical extension and research questions rather than completed empirical validation. These sources therefore support the proposition without establishing a general predictive theory or a validated recipe for producing institutional change.
